1	# The machine and its prices
2	
3	Facts about this container and the tools on it, with numbers. They were checked against `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` (its test-harness and container sections), the files it cites, `explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md`, the header lines of the two measurement scripts and the last full run's summary. Times are wall-clock seconds on this machine; a run beside other work is slower.
4	
5	## The machine
6	
7	- **CPUs: 4** (Intel Xeon at 2.8 GHz, `nproc` = 4); about 15 GB of memory (`free -g`, measured now). OpenJDK 25. The suites pin one interpreter thread per JVM (`FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, set in `build.xml`), so the four cores are used by running several JVMs at once (`ant testFast` runs four tracks that occupy the four cores; `ant testSystem` is split into four shards).
8	- **Heaps.** `bin/fortress` gives its JVM 256 MB unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set; the `ant testSystem` harness 768 MB; `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, which every measurement script expects to be sourced, sets 4 GB.
9	- **Disk.** Every run that imports a grammar writes a 5.8 MB parser directory to `/tmp` (`/tmp/fortress<random>rats`) and never deletes it; 723 of them (4.2 GB) once filled the disk allowance and broke a tool's output with "no space left on device". Sourcing `explorations/experiment/env.sh` removes them; check `df` before a long run.
10	- **Build commands.** `export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64`, `export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH`, `export FORTRESS_HOME=<repo root>`, `unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, then `ant compileAll` from the repository root. `ant compileAll` deletes the whole `default_repository/caches` including the tracked file `default_repository/caches/global.map`: restore it with `git checkout -- default_repository/caches/global.map` after every `ant compileAll`, and never commit its deletion. A compiled run (`fortress compile`, `fortress run`) needs the library compiled in order after a rebuild (AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary, CompilerAlgebra, CompilerSystem); stale caches give a misleading `NoSuchMethodError`. Walk does not need that order; its first run warms its own caches.
11	
12	## The times
13	
14	- `ant compileAll`: 57 s in the last full run; 82 s on a fresh checkout; 25 to 40 s on an already built tree after a small edit.
15	- The library compile (the five components in order, after `ant compileAll`): 108 to 112 s (AnyType 17, CompilerBuiltin 63, CompilerLibrary 27, CompilerAlgebra 2, CompilerSystem 2); one component alone 2 to 63 s. A base built from nothing, `ant compileAll` plus the library compile plus one walk run, is about 200 s.
16	- `ant testFast`: 635 s (10 min 35 s) in the last full run, 1,782 tests, 0 failures; the longest single suite in it takes about 440 s, so more parallelism does not shorten it much.
17	- `ant testSystem`: 243 s (4 min 3 s) in the last full run, 504 tests in four shards, 0 failures.
18	- The checker-count measurement (`explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]`; it counts the errors the compiled checker reports on the library before each api's early return, 1 now): about 20 s alone on an idle machine when first measured (the library has grown since); 139 s when it ran beside other jobs.
19	- The distance measurement (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]`; it runs every phase of the compiled checker over all twelve apis and twelve components in one JVM on one busy core and counts every distinct error, 340 now): 1,212 s (20 min) in the last full run, 732 s of it on `FortressLibrary` alone; 789 s on an idle machine earlier; 14 to 24 minutes under load.
20	- One walk run of a small program: about 8 s on cold caches. A compile of a small program: about 5 s, its run about 1 s.
21	
22	## Copying a build, and running the old code
23	
24	- **A built tree can be copied into a new worktree in about 3 s**: `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]`. The base worktree must have been built once (`ant compileAll`, the restore of `global.map`, the library compile). The copy (206 MB: build 40 MB, caches 36 MB) runs walk and the compiled path without building anything, and its paths are translated for the new location.
25	- **The base's code runs beside the new code** with a private cache folder: `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...` (for example `old-fortress.sh <base-build> <dir>/old-caches compile P.fss`, then `... run P`, or `... P.fss` for walk). The private folder is a copy of the base's caches, 36 MB made in 0.04 s; the run writes nothing that stays in the base build. Keep the private folder and the programs outside the base build.
26	
27	## The agents and their prices
28	
29	- **How many agents run at once: 2.** The multi-agent harness (the script-driven tool that starts agents in parallel or in sequence) runs two agents at a time on this box; more wait for a free slot.
30	- **An agent's floor is about 45,000 tokens before it does anything** (system prompt, tools, first message). Prompt caching across parallel agents covers the system prompt and tools only (about 33,000 tokens read) and not the first user message (about 11,000 tokens written by each agent). Agents started with an identical whole prompt share the cache (the second reads what the first wrote and writes nothing); a prompt that differs only in its last line shares only the system prompt and tools (about 35,000 tokens read) and writes the rest again.
31	- **The prompt cache lives 1 hour for the main session and 5 minutes for a subagent.** A call within the life reads the cache and renews it, so a wait taken in steps shorter than the life costs a cache read per step. A wait longer than the life makes the next call write the agent's whole context again with no cache read: a subagent holding a 250,000-token context that waits 8 minutes on a build writes 250,000 tokens at its next call.
32	- **The Bash tool's time limit is 10 minutes** (600 s) for a foreground call (default 2 minutes); the call is killed at the limit. A longer command runs in the background and is polled.
33	- **The project counts cost as tokens written**: cache writes and new input. Cache reads are not counted.
34	- **Three model tiers are available: Opus, Sonnet and Fable.** Fable is the strongest and draws on a separate, scarcer weekly pool; Sonnet is the cheapest. An agent that names no model inherits the session's.
35	- **An agent call can come back empty.** The harness returns null for an agent it has marked failed, even when the agent delivered its structured result first (the platform's safety filter has ended agents this way); a design must expect it.
36	- **The platform stops the session's process after about 13 hours** (12 h 58 min of continuous running; the stops fall at 46,636 to 46,660 s) and restarts it in resume mode within seconds. The restart kills every running harness run and every running agent; the conversation, the worktrees, the transcripts and each run's journal survive. **A run of the harness is resumed from its journal**: agents that had finished keep their results, an unfinished agent runs again from its start. The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of the run's agent calls in call order, so it needs the script and its arguments exactly as at launch and the agents called in the same order. A VM restart and an interrupt of the session's current turn also kill running agents; a resume from the journal recovers the harness's agents that had finished.

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

97	## The two worlds
98	
99	The tree contains two nearly-disjoint executions of Fortress, and most
100	confusion comes from mixing them up:
101	
102	| | interpreter ("walk") | bytecode compiler |
103	|---|---|---|
104	| era | 2003-lineage, mature | 2010–2012, the team's final push, incomplete |
105	| entry | `fortress <file>.fss` | `fortress compile <file>.fss` + `fortress run <component>` |
106	| libraries | `Library/` + `LibraryBuiltin/` (FortressBuiltin, NativeArray, ...) | `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra`, `CompilerSystem`, `GeneratorLibrary` |
107	| native mechanism | `builtinPrimitive("com.sun...glue.prim.X")` in .fss | `import java com.sun...nativeHelpers.{...}` in .fss |
108	| native String type | glue-level FString | `CompilerBuiltin.JavaString` / `StringVector` (foreign map in `NamingCzar`) |
109	| tests | `ProjectFortress/tests/` via `ant testSystem` | `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` via `ant testFast` etc. |
110	
111	The mode switch is `com.sun.fortress.compiler.WellKnownNames`:
112	`useInterpreterLibraries()` / `useCompilerLibraries()` swap the meaning of
113	"the builtin library" (`FortressBuiltin` vs `CompilerBuiltin`) and "the
114	standard library" (`FortressLibrary` vs `CompilerLibrary`). `Shell.subMain`
115	calls one or the other per subcommand (`walk` vs `compile`/`run`/`link`).
116	
117	Consequences:
118	- A `.fss` file is generally written for ONE world. `import java ...` means
119	  compiler-only; `builtinPrimitive` means interpreter-only.
120	- An *api name* used by both worlds is trouble: apis resolve by name along a
121	  single shared source path (see below). This is exactly what broke the six
122	  interpreter tests in the 2012 endgame (`api System` shadowed — see
123	  test-baseline postscript) and why the compiler apis are `Compiler*`-prefixed.
124	
125	## The pipeline, phase by phase (verified 2026-09-08 from `compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java` and `Shell.java`)
126	
127	Both execution paths share one phase list and differ only at the end. Parse (`parser/`, Rats!) produces the AST (`nodes/`); then PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE (names bound to declarations), GRAMMAR (syntax extensions), PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, TYPECHECK (`scala_src/typechecker/`, writes a static type on every expression; no new representation), DESUGAR (comprehensions and big operators to `generate` calls with reduction objects, coercions, chained comparisons, getters/setters), then OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN on the compiler path (`compilerPhaseOrder`, which also has INTEGERLITERALFOLDING before TYPECHECK) or OVERLOADREWRITE_FOR_INTERPRETER on the interpreter path (`interpreterPhaseOrder`). The AST is the only intermediate representation from parse to bytecode; there is no lower IR and no optimizing middle.
128	
129	The TYPECHECK phase is in the interpreter's list but is a no-op there: `walk` calls `setScala(false)` and the checking flag `fortress.compile.typecheck` defaults to false, and `StaticChecker` returns the tree untouched when off. `compile`/`build` set it on. Consequently the interpreter runs untyped desugared trees and accepts spec-illegal programs (e.g. `Value extends Number` against `Number comprises {RR64}`), and there is no command-line switch to enable checking for `walk`.
130	
131	What the code generator does with the static types: every Fortress type is lowered to a JVM reference type (traits to interfaces, objects to classes, `RR64` to the runtime class `FRR64` via `NamingCzar`; `CodeGen.java` emits no `DADD`), every overloaded name gets one generated dispatch method that tests argument types from most to least specific (symmetric multimethod dispatch on run-time types), and generic declarations are compiled once as templates whose instantiations (`Box⟦RR64⟧`, oxford brackets from `Naming.java`) are stamped out by `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java` at first use by ASM rewriting of the template bytes; instantiation renames, it does not change representation. Emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6 because the load-time rewriting pipeline does not maintain stack-map frames and the JVM verifier may fall back to type inference only at that version. The `value` modifier on objects (spec: immutable fields, no identity) has no representation meaning in codegen.
132	
133	## Name resolution: fortress.source.path
134	
135	`default_repository/configuration` (overridable via `local_repository/`,
136	`~/.fortress/`, `./.fortress/`, env vars, or `-D` flags) defines:
137	
138	    fortress.source.path=;.;${_fr}/LibraryBuiltin;${FORTRESS_AUTOHOME}/Library;${_fr}/test_library
139	
140	- Leading `;` sets the separator (Windows compat). `.` (cwd!) is searched
141	  FIRST, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, then `Library/`.
142	- `import Foo` finds the first `Foo.fsi`/`Foo.fss` on that path. First hit
143	  wins — a file earlier on the path silently shadows a later one, and cwd can
144	  shadow everything (mind where you run from).
145	- The interpreter requires filename (sans suffix) == component/api name.
146	
147	## Cache anatomy and hygiene
148	
149	`default_repository/caches/` (gitignored by path, as is
150	`ProjectFortress/test-caches/`; a cache written anywhere else, such as a
151	probe's own `-Dfortress.caches` directory, is not ignored):
152	- `analyzed_cache/`, `*parsed_cache/` — front-end analysis, shared-ish
153	  between worlds; the main source of cross-world contamination.
154	- `interpreter_cache/`, `environment_cache/` — interpreter side.
155	- `bytecode_cache/` — compiler output: one jar per compiled component;
156	  library components get api-qualified names (`fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`).
157	- `nativewrapper_cache/` — generated wrappers for `import java` natives.
158	
159	Rules learned the hard way:
160	- **When in doubt, wipe**: `rm -rf default_repository/caches/*`. Stale or
161	  order-inconsistent caches produce *misleading* runtime errors
162	  (`NoSuchMethodError: CompilerBuiltin.println(...)`,
163	  `NoSuchMethodError: ...asJavaString()`, `Unable to read serialized data
164	  ... recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink`). These
165	  are cache problems, not compiler bugs.
166	- After editing any `Library/`/`LibraryBuiltin/` `.fss`, wipe — edits are
167	  otherwise invisible (cached analysis wins).
168	- **Compile order matters** on a fresh cache, because `fortress compile` of a
169	  program does NOT emit the builtin-library jars, and the runtime classloader
170	  then falls back to the **bootstrap stubs** in `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`
171	  (ant-compiled from checked-in `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/*.java` —
172	  a *frozen, older* snapshot of CompilerBuiltin!). Symptom: NoSuchMethodError
173	  on a method that plainly exists in CompilerBuiltin.fss. Recipe:
174	
175	      cd ProjectFortress
176	      ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss
177	      ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss
178	      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss
179	      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss
180	      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss
181	      ../bin/fortress compile <program>.fss
182	      ../bin/fortress run <component> [args...]
183	
184	  The JUnit harness gets this right because `CompilerJUTest` starts with
185	  `Shell.resetRepository()` and compiles the world in dependency order.
186	
187	## Toolchain traps (JDK rungs)
188	
189	- **build.xml's javac tasks originally set `source=` but never `target=`**
190	  (and three set neither). Harmless on JDK 8 (target defaulted to 8); on
191	  JDK 11 target defaulted to 11 → v55 classfiles with invokedynamic string
192	  concat → ASM 3.1's ClassReader (used by `ForeignJava.findClass` for every
193	  `import java ...`) dies with `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, failing all
194	  compiler-path tests while testSystem stays green. Fixed by pinning
195	  `target="${javaSourceVersion}"` on all 8 javac tasks (commit fdd4a57c2).
196	  Diagnosis trick: a 20-line probe compiling against
197	  `third_party/asm/asm-all-3.1.jar` + `javap -v | grep major` pinpoints
198	  exactly which classfile ASM chokes on. (Surprise: JDK 11's *platform*
199	  classes parse fine under `SKIP_DEBUG|SKIP_FRAMES|SKIP_CODE`; it was our
200	  own freshly compiled v55 output that broke.)
201	- `default_repository/caches/global.map` is a **tracked** file at the caches
202	  root, so `rm -rf default_repository/caches/*` deletes tracked content —
203	  wipe with `rm -rf default_repository/caches/*_cache
204	  default_repository/caches/logs` instead, or `git checkout` it back.
205	
206	## Generated code
207	
208	- Churn in the generated sources after a build is a regression to investigate,
209	  never noise to revert.
210	- AST nodes (`src/com/sun/fortress/nodes/`, 1000+ files),
211	  `scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, `Library/FortressAst.fsi/fss` are all
212	  generated by astgen from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` (build
213	  target `makeAST`). They are checked in; ant's uptodate check compares
214	  mtimes, so a fresh checkout looks current. If scalac errors show arity
215	  mismatches in `S*Pattern` nodes: `touch ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast
216	  && ant compileAll`.
217	- Parser (`parser/*.java` from Rats! grammars), `precedence_resolver/
218	  Operators.java` (from unicode data) — same pattern.
219	
220	## Test harness mechanics
221	
222	- Targets: `testFast` (unit + compiler suites, ~12 min, excludes interpreter
223	  system tests), `testSystem` (interpreter, 382 tests, ~2 min),
224	  `testLibrary`, `testCompiler`, `testNotPassing` (expected failures),
225	  `testDemos`, nightly variants. Plain-text results land in
226	  `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/TEST-<class>.txt`.
227	- `.test` files (in `compiler_tests/` etc.) are property files driving
228	  `FileTests`: keys like `compile`, `run`, `tests=`, `compile_err_equals=`
229	  decide which phases run and what output to expect. `run`-tests execute the
230	  compiled program via the `bin/run` script in a subprocess.
231	- To reproduce one interpreter test: `../bin/fortress tests/<Name>.fss`
232	  (from `ProjectFortress/`). Failures print the real diagnostic that the
233	  JUnit boilerplate hides.
234	- Suite runs reset/repopulate `default_repository/caches` — don't interleave
235	  ad-hoc compiles with a running suite, and don't trust cache state after one.
236	
237	## Git archaeology techniques
238	
239	- **The history has a parallel root**: `5a68404` (David Chase, 2012-07-19,
240	  4372 files) is a parentless import later merged by `575fe64`. Any
241	  `git log <base>..HEAD -- <file>` therefore lists `5a68404` for almost
242	  every file — useless for "who changed what since June". Use **content
243	  comparison** instead: `git diff --quiet <base> HEAD -- <file>` and
244	  `git show <base>:<file> | cmp - <other-tree>/<file>`.
245	- The twelve pre-2016 branches are hg named-branch relics; the 2008 research
246	  branches were squash-merged into trunk, so fine-grained authorship exists
247	  only on the branch heads. Full survey with per-branch verdicts: see the
248	  session notes / ask before deleting anything.
249	- hg conversion quirks: empty "Starting/Closing branch X" marker commits;
250	  `.hgignore` still in tree; David Chase's 2012-01-20 branch-closing sweep.
251	
252	## Environment gotchas (cloud container)
253	
254	- Current rung JDK 25 (`/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64`; 8/11/17/21 also
255	  gated green); `unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` or the proxy's trust-store flags
256	  pollute every JVM fork.
257	- `web.archive.org` and `labs.oracle.com` are blocked by network policy —
258	  research PDFs must be uploaded into the session by Pavol. Archived *pages*
259	  (not PDFs) can be read via the pure.md relay; see the method note in
260	  `research/extracts/fortress-websites-wayback.md`.
261	- Gitignored files (e.g. `research/decks/*.pdf`) do not survive the
262	  container; only commits and pushes persist.
